concepts.title: The JSONB Type: When to Reach for It
concepts.description: JSONB lets a column hold variable-shape data that you can query and index almost like a normal column. The flexibility costs you every constraint, type check, and typo-detecting error a normalized column would give you for free, and that trade-off is what to reason about before reaching for it.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between PostgreSQL's JSON and JSONB storage formats and why JSONB is almost always the right default for querying.
Query JSONB data using the ->, ->>, #>, #>>, and containment (@>) operators.
Create a GIN index on a JSONB column and explain what specific query patterns it does and doesn't accelerate.
Compare storing data as JSONB versus normalized columns/tables using concrete criteria: schema stability, need for constraints, and query patterns.
Identify the anti-pattern of using JSONB to avoid schema design for data that is actually stable and well-known, and explain the concrete costs of that choice.

sections.heading: JSON vs. JSONB: Two Different Storage Strategies
sections.body:
PostgreSQL has two types for storing JSON documents in a single column, and the difference is about storage strategy, not the data model. The `json` type stores the original text byte for byte, preserving whitespace, key order, and duplicate keys, and re-parses that text every time a query looks inside it. The `jsonb` type parses the document once, at insert time, into a decomposed binary structure. It keeps no whitespace or key order, and for duplicate keys only the last one survives. That costs a little extra on every insert and pays it back on every read, since queries work on the already-parsed structure.

For nearly every use case `jsonb` is the right default. Reach for `json` only if you need the exact original text, for example to round-trip a document as a client sent it because key order or formatting matters to a downstream consumer. `jsonb` is also the only one of the two that supports the indexing covered later in this concept, and most PostgreSQL codebases use it exclusively.

sections.heading: Digging Into a JSONB Document: The Core Operators
sections.body:
A handful of operators cover most JSONB querying. `->` extracts a value by key or array index and returns it as `jsonb`, so it can be chained for nested access. `->>` does the same but returns `text`, which is what you want at the end of a chain when you compare against a plain string or number. `#>` and `#>>` are the path-based versions: they take an array of keys and indexes to descend several levels at once instead of chaining `->` calls.

```sql
SELECT
    data -> 'address' ->> 'city' AS city,
    data #>> '{address,zip}' AS zip
FROM customers;
```

The **containment operator**, `@>`, asks whether the left JSONB value contains the right one as a subset. It is the operator most often used for filtering, and the one a GIN index (covered next) is built to accelerate:

```sql
SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"type": "click"}'::jsonb;
```

One sharp edge to know up front: a typo'd or missing key with `->>` does not raise an error. It returns SQL `NULL`, as if the key legitimately held no value. A typo'd column name on a normalized table, by contrast, is rejected immediately with `column "..." does not exist`. This silent NULL is one of JSONB's ongoing costs. A bug in a key name doesn't announce itself; it just returns nothing, and the anti-pattern section below comes back to it.

sections.heading: Indexing JSONB with GIN
sections.body:
An ordinary B-tree index on a `jsonb` column only supports comparisons against the *entire* document, which is rarely useful, since you almost never ask whether a row's JSON blob equals some other whole blob. The index PostgreSQL provides for JSONB is **GIN** (Generalized Inverted Index), which indexes the individual keys and values *inside* the document. That makes containment (`@>`) and key-existence (`?`, `?&`, `?|`) queries fast without scanning every row:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_events_payload ON events USING GIN (payload);

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"type": "click"}'::jsonb;
-- Bitmap Index Scan using idx_events_payload
--   Index Cond: (payload @> '{"type": "click"}'::jsonb)
```

A GIN index on `jsonb` has two operator classes, and the choice matters. The default, `jsonb_ops`, supports `@>`, `?`, `?&`, and `?|` (containment plus key existence), at the cost of a larger index. The `jsonb_path_ops` variant (`CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN (payload jsonb_path_ops)`) supports *only* `@>`, but gives a smaller, usually faster index for that one operator. If you pick `jsonb_path_ops` and your application also uses the `?` operators, those queries quietly fall back to a sequential scan: the index exists but doesn't support the operator being used, just like a B-tree index that doesn't match a query's expression, covered in the indexing module.

If you always filter on one key, a plain B-tree expression index is often smaller and faster than GIN: `CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload ->> 'type'));` serves `WHERE payload ->> 'type' = 'click'`, though not `@>` queries.

sections.heading: When JSONB Is the Right Tool
sections.body:
JSONB earns its place for data whose shape varies or is unpredictable per row, where giving every possible field its own column would mean an enormous sparse table (mostly NULLs) or a schema migration each time a new field appears. Common cases: third-party webhook payloads, where each event type from an external provider has its own shape that you don't control and don't want to model column by column; user-defined custom attributes, where end users attach arbitrary key-value pairs with no fixed schema by design; and event or analytics payloads, where different event types carry different fields and the *set* of event types keeps growing over the life of the product.

In all of these, the data is usually stored and retrieved as a whole document more often than it is filtered by one inner field. When it is filtered by inner fields, those fields are themselves part of the variability, not a small fixed set present on every row. That is the shape JSONB suits, and it is a legitimate tool, not a fallback for when modeling feels inconvenient. One cost to keep in mind for large documents: changing a single key rewrites the whole JSONB value, so frequently updating one small field inside a big document is more expensive than updating a normal column. Updates themselves are written with functions and operators, for example `UPDATE customers SET metadata = jsonb_set(metadata, '{address,city}', '"Dallas"') WHERE id = 1;` to replace one nested value, or `metadata = metadata || '{"vip": false}'` to merge keys into the top level.

sections.heading: The Anti-Pattern: 'Just Throw It in a JSONB Column'
sections.body:
The opposite situation, a field present on nearly every row, with one known type, that participates in the business's invariants, belongs in a normalized column, not in a JSONB blob 'for flexibility.' A typical anti-pattern is storing `customer_email`, `customer_name`, and `order_status` in a single JSONB `data` column on an `orders` table, on the reasoning that it avoids a migration if a new field shows up later.

The costs are immediate. No `NOT NULL`, `CHECK`, `FOREIGN KEY`, or `UNIQUE` constraint can be declared on a value inside a JSONB document, so `order_status` can hold `'Shiped'` (a typo) or any other string with nothing rejecting it, while a real column with `CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'shipped', 'cancelled'))` refuses the write. Every value read back is `jsonb` or `text`, so numeric comparisons need explicit casts (`(data->>'amount')::numeric > 100`) that are easy to forget and that compare as text if you do. The planner's statistics are also much weaker for values buried in a JSONB document than for a column with its own per-column statistics, which can mean worse plans for exactly the filtering this data gets. And a typo in a key name returns a NULL instead of an error, which for a field as central as an order's status is a dangerous failure mode: a bug that produces wrong results with no error message pointing at it.

The middle ground most real schemas land on is to normalize the columns that are stable, well known, and needed for business logic and constraints, and keep a JSONB column *alongside* them for the sparse, variable extra attributes. You get constraints and type safety where they matter and flexibility where it is needed, instead of choosing one strategy for the entire row.

examples.title: Basic JSONB Querying: ->, ->>, and #>>
examples.explanation: `->` returns a `jsonb` value, which is why `metadata -> 'address'` still shows the nested object: it is meant to be chained, as the next line does by following it with `->>` to pull out `city` as text. `#>>` reaches several levels deep in one step with a path array, equivalent to `metadata -> 'address' ->> 'zip'` but more compact. The last line is a common source of subtle bugs: `metadata ->> 'vip'` returns the *text* `'true'`, not the boolean `true`. Writing `metadata ->> 'vip' = true` fails with `operator does not exist: text = boolean`. Cast it, `(metadata ->> 'vip')::boolean`, or stay in jsonb and compare with `metadata -> 'vip' = 'true'::jsonb`.

examples.title: GIN Index Turning a Sequential Scan Into an Index Scan
examples.explanation: Before the GIN index exists, the only way to evaluate `payload @> '{"type": "click"}'::jsonb` is to check every row's payload, like any other unindexed predicate. GIN indexes the individual keys and values inside each document, so it can find candidate rows without checking every row. The `Recheck Cond` line is a normal part of GIN bitmap scans: PostgreSQL re-checks the exact condition on the heap rows the index returned, because the index can include false positives. It does not mean the index failed to help. This index was built with the default `jsonb_ops` class, so it would also speed up the `?`, `?&`, and `?|` key-existence operators, which the narrower `jsonb_path_ops` would not.

examples.title: The Silent NULL From a Typo'd Key
examples.code:
-- data has a key "status", not "Status"
SELECT id, data ->> 'Status' AS status FROM orders WHERE id = 1;
-- status
-- --------
-- (NULL)     <-- no error, just NULL, even though "status" clearly exists

-- Compare to a normalized column with the same typo:
SELECT id, "Status" FROM orders WHERE id = 1;
-- ERROR:  column "Status" does not exist
-- HINT:  Perhaps you meant to reference the column "status".
examples.explanation: `->>` (and `->`, `#>`, `#>>`) never raise an error for a missing or mistyped key. They return SQL NULL, because from JSONB's point of view a missing key and an absent value look the same. That is the ongoing cost of storing structured data as JSONB: a typo in a key name produces NULL results that can slip through unnoticed, while the same mistake against a normalized column fails at query time with an actionable error, and PostgreSQL even suggests the correct column name in the HINT. The JSONB version of the bug can sit in production code for a long time because nothing about it looks broken; it just returns NULL wherever the typo'd key is read.

misconceptions.description: JSONB in PostgreSQL is basically a schemaless, NoSQL-style escape hatch, so you can just put anything in it and skip schema design entirely.
misconceptions.clarification: JSONB supports variable-shape data well, but it has costs: no way to declare NOT NULL, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, or UNIQUE constraints on a value inside a document, a typo'd key returns NULL instead of an error, every value comes back as jsonb or text and needs explicit casts for numeric comparisons, and the planner has weaker statistics for values inside a document than for a dedicated column. It is a good fit for data that varies in shape, not a substitute for modeling stable, well-known attributes that carry business logic as proper columns.

misconceptions.description: A GIN index on a JSONB column makes every kind of query into that column fast, regardless of which operator the query uses.
misconceptions.clarification: A GIN index accelerates the operators it was built to support. The default jsonb_ops operator class covers containment (@>) and key existence (?, ?&, ?|); the narrower jsonb_path_ops covers only @>, in exchange for a smaller, faster index for that operator. Neither variant helps a query that uses some other operator. A query using ? against an index built with jsonb_path_ops gets no benefit from it and falls back to a full scan, as if no index existed.

exercises.prompt: A `webhook_events` table stores third-party payloads of varying shape in a `payload JSONB` column. Write a query that finds every event where the payload's `"type"` key equals `"payment.failed"`, and write the index that would make this query fast at scale.
hints: The containment operator @> asks whether the left JSONB value contains the right one as a subset -- a single key-value pair on the right is exactly this kind of subset check.
A plain B-tree index on payload only supports whole-document equality, which isn't what this query needs -- GIN is the index type built for containment queries into a document's contents.
CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN (payload) with no operator class specified uses the default jsonb_ops, which supports @>.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The query uses @>, asking whether each row's payload contains {"type": "payment.failed"} as a subset. That is true for any payload with a "type" key holding that value, whatever other keys the provider's event includes. A GIN index on payload (default jsonb_ops class, which supports @>) lets PostgreSQL find matching rows through the index instead of checking every payload, the same benefit a B-tree gives an equality filter on a normal column, but working over the contents of a variable-shape document.

exercises.prompt: A team stores `customer_name` and `order_status` inside a JSONB `data` column on `orders`, reasoning it avoids future migrations. A bug let an order get stored with `order_status` set to `'Shiped'` (a typo), and no error was ever raised anywhere. Explain why this was possible and redesign the schema to prevent it.
hints: What kind of constraint would normally reject an invalid value in a fixed, known set of allowed values -- and can that constraint be declared against a value living inside a JSONB document?
order_status is present on presumably every order and has a small, fixed set of valid values -- does that sound like genuinely variable-shape data, or a normal, stable column?
Pull order_status (and similarly stable fields like customer_name) out into real columns, and add a CHECK constraint enumerating the valid status values.
exercises.solutionExplanation: A CHECK constraint cannot be declared on a value nested inside a JSONB document, because PostgreSQL's constraint system works on columns, not on keys inside a document. A typo like 'Shiped' was therefore accepted as a valid JSONB string, indistinguishable from any other text. customer_name and order_status belong as real columns: they are present on essentially every order, have known types, and order_status has a small fixed set of valid values that a business rule depends on. With both pulled out into columns and CHECK (order_status IN (...)) on the status column, the typo can't be stored: the INSERT is rejected with a clear error instead of succeeding with bad data that nothing downstream would catch. A variable extra_attributes JSONB column can stay alongside them for per-order metadata that doesn't fit a fixed schema, without weakening the constraints on the fields that do.

assessments.prompt: A table needs to store a `status` field present on every row, with exactly five allowed values enforced by business logic, alongside a small set of optional, provider-specific fields that vary depending on which third-party integration created the row. What's the most appropriate design?
options: Create five separate boolean columns, one per possible status value.
Store everything, including status, inside a single JSONB column for maximum flexibility.
Store status as JSONB specifically so it can be indexed with GIN, and keep the variable fields as normalized columns.
Make status a normalized TEXT column with a CHECK constraint enumerating the five allowed values, and store the genuinely variable provider-specific fields in a separate JSONB column.
assessments.explanation: The two shapes of data call for different tools. status is present on every row and has a small fixed set of valid values, so it belongs in a column where a CHECK constraint can enforce it, which only a real column supports. The provider-specific fields vary in shape from row to row, which is what JSONB suits. The “Store everything, including status, inside a single…” option gives up constraint enforcement on status for no benefit, since status isn't variable. The “Create five separate boolean columns, one per…” option models a single mutually exclusive status worse than one column with a CHECK constraint, and ignores the variable fields. The “Store status as JSONB specifically…” option inverts the assignment: the variable fields belong in JSONB and the stable, fixed-set status belongs in a constrained column. A GIN index isn't what status needs either, since it is filtered by simple equality.

assessments.prompt: Explain the concrete trade-offs between storing a piece of data as JSONB versus as a normalized column, referencing constraints, type safety, and indexing specifically -- and describe what kind of data should tip the decision toward each.
assessments.modelAnswer: The decision comes down to whether a piece of data is stable and well known in shape or varies from row to row. A normalized column gives you three things JSONB cannot provide for a value inside a document. First, database-enforced constraints (NOT NULL, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE) that make invalid states impossible to store, rather than discouraged by convention. Second, type safety: a column has one declared type and comparisons work naturally, whereas every value extracted from JSONB comes back as jsonb or text and needs explicit casts for numeric or boolean comparisons, a step that is easy to forget and that then compares as text instead of failing. Third, precise per-column statistics that help the planner, which are much weaker for values nested in a JSONB document. A normalized column also fails loudly on a typo, since a misspelled column name raises an immediate error, while a misspelled key inside JSONB returns NULL and produces wrong results with no error pointing at the cause. JSONB earns its place when the data's shape is unpredictable per row in a way normalization can't sensibly capture: third-party webhook payloads whose shape you don't control, user-defined custom attributes with no fixed schema, or event payloads where different event types carry different fields and the set of types keeps growing. There, a GIN index on the JSONB column (using @> for containment or ?/?&/?| for key existence, depending on the operator class) gives reasonably fast querying into the variable structure without a rigid schema for data that doesn't have one. The anti-pattern to avoid is using JSONB to skip schema design for data that is stable and known, such as a status field with five valid values, a customer's name, or an amount used in arithmetic, because that trades away constraints, type safety, clear error messages, and planner statistics for flexibility the data never needed.

assessments.prompt: What is the key structural difference between PostgreSQL's `json` and `jsonb` types?
options: json has been removed from current PostgreSQL versions entirely; jsonb is now the only valid type name.
jsonb stores data as plain text identical to json, but under a different type name kept only for backward compatibility.

json stores the exact original text verbatim -- preserving whitespace, key order, and duplicate keys -- and re-parses that text on every query; jsonb parses the document once, at insert time, into a decomposed binary structure with no preserved formatting or duplicate keys, trading a small insert-time cost for faster reads.
json supports containment queries with @>, while jsonb does not support any operators at all.
assessments.explanation: json is a thin wrapper over the original text, re-parsed on every access, while jsonb does the parsing once at write time and stores a decomposed binary structure that every read can use. The “json supports containment queries with @>, while…” option reverses which type has the rich operator and indexing support: that is jsonb. The “json has been removed from current PostgreSQL…” option is false; json remains a valid type, just rarely the better default. The “jsonb stores data as plain text identical…” option ignores the binary decomposition that makes jsonb different from, and generally faster to query than, json.

assessments.prompt: A GIN index is created with `CREATE INDEX idx_events_payload ON events USING GIN (payload jsonb_path_ops);`. A query then filters using `payload ? 'type'` (the key-existence operator). What happens?
options: The query falls back to a sequential scan, because jsonb_path_ops only supports the containment operator @> -- not the ?, ?&, or ?| key-existence operators -- so the index exists but simply doesn't support the operator being used.
The index is automatically and silently rebuilt using the default jsonb_ops operator class the first time an unsupported operator is used against it.
PostgreSQL raises an error, refusing to execute a query that uses an operator unsupported by the chosen operator class.
The query uses the index efficiently, since jsonb_path_ops supports every JSONB operator, including key existence.
assessments.explanation: jsonb_path_ops is narrower than the default jsonb_ops: it supports only @>, in exchange for a smaller, faster index for that operator. A query using ? against a jsonb_path_ops index gets no help from it and falls back to a full scan, like a B-tree index that doesn't match a query's expression. The “The query uses the index efficiently, since…” option overstates jsonb_path_ops's coverage. The “PostgreSQL raises an error, refusing to execute…” option invents an error: an unsupported operator just doesn't use the index, and the query still runs. The “The index is automatically and silently rebuilt…” option invents an automatic rebuild; an operator class mismatch is a quiet performance problem that never corrects itself.

assessments.prompt: A query filters using `(data->>'amount') > '100'`, comparing the extracted value against a quoted literal without casting it to a numeric type. What is the risk here?
options: The comparison always evaluates to NULL when comparing text against a number, silently excluding every row from any query that omits the cast.
data->>'amount' returns text, so the comparison is silently performed as a text (lexicographic) comparison rather than a numeric one.
PostgreSQL raises an immediate type-mismatch error, refusing to run the comparison at all.
PostgreSQL automatically infers, from the key name 'amount', that the value should be treated as numeric, and casts it correctly without being asked.
assessments.explanation: ->> always returns text, and comparing text with a quoted literal using > is a lexicographic string comparison, not a numeric one. It produces results that look plausible but are wrong: '9' > '100' is true as strings even though 9 is less than 100. The “PostgreSQL raises an immediate type-mismatch error, refusing…” option is false for this query, which is what makes it dangerous: it runs and returns a result, just not the intended one. (With an unquoted number, `(data->>'amount') > 100`, PostgreSQL does raise `operator does not exist: text > integer`. The silent case appears with quoted literals or text-typed parameters.) The “PostgreSQL automatically infers, from the key name…” option invents type inference from key names, which PostgreSQL does not do. The “The comparison always evaluates to NULL…” option invents a blanket NULL rule; this comparison resolves to an actual, often wrong, text comparison.

concepts.title: Full-Text Search with tsvector and tsquery
concepts.description: LIKE and ILIKE only match literal substrings. A leading wildcard forces a full scan, and a search for 'run' misses 'running'. PostgreSQL's tsvector/tsquery machinery stems and normalizes text into lexemes, supports GIN indexing at scale, and ranks results by relevance instead of returning an arbitrary unordered match.
learningObjectives: Explain why LIKE/ILIKE pattern matching is a poor substitute for full-text search, specifically regarding indexing, stemming, and relevance.
Convert text into a tsvector with to_tsvector, and explain what stemming, stop-word removal, and lexeme positions each contribute.
Construct search terms with to_tsquery and plainto_tsquery, and explain when each is the appropriate choice.
Use the @@ match operator to filter rows, and create a GIN index on a generated tsvector column to make full-text search fast at scale.
Use ts_rank to order results by relevance, and explain why matching and ranking are two separate costs in a full-text search query.

sections.heading: Why LIKE Isn't Full-Text Search
sections.body:
`LIKE`/`ILIKE` answer one narrow question: does this substring appear in this text, in this form? That causes several problems once 'search' is the goal. A leading-wildcard pattern like `ILIKE '%phone%'` cannot use a standard B-tree index, as the indexing module explained: a B-tree's sorted order only helps when a match is a contiguous range, and 'contains this substring anywhere' is not, so every search is a full sequential scan however large the table.

Beyond performance, LIKE has no linguistic awareness: searching for `'run'` won't match a document containing only `'running'`, because those are different literal substrings, though a human would treat them as related. It has no concept of relevance, so a document that mentions the term once in passing is as good a match as one centered on it. And it matches inside unrelated words: `LIKE '%cat%'` matches `'category'` and `'concatenate'` as readily as `'cat'`, returning noise alongside real matches. PostgreSQL's full-text search (`tsvector`, `tsquery`, and the `@@` match operator) is built to solve each of these.

sections.heading: tsvector: A Preprocessed, Searchable Representation of Text
sections.body:
`to_tsvector(config, text)` turns ordinary text into a `tsvector`: a sorted list of normalized word forms (**lexemes**) with their positions in the original text. It applies three steps. It lowercases everything; it removes common **stop words** ('the', 'and', 'were', 'a') that carry almost no search value and would match nearly every document; and it **stems** each remaining word to a root form, so 'running' and 'runs' both reduce to 'run'. (Stemmers are rule-based, so irregular forms like 'ran' are left alone.)

```sql
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The quick foxes were running through the forest');
--                          to_tsvector
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------
--  'forest':8 'fox':3 'quick':2 'run':5
```

'The', 'were', 'through', and the second 'the' are gone (stop words), 'foxes' became 'fox' and 'running' became 'run' (stemming), and each surviving lexeme carries its position in the original text, counting the removed words too, which is what later enables phrase and proximity matching. The `'english'` argument names a text search **configuration**, a bundle of a stop-word list and a stemming dictionary for one language. Other languages have their own configurations, and the choice matters: a document processed with one configuration and searched with another may fail to line up, a point the exercises return to.

sections.heading: tsquery: Structured Search Terms, and @@ Matching
sections.body:
A `tsquery` is a small query tree of lexemes combined with logical operators: `&` (AND), `|` (OR), `!` (NOT), and `<->` (followed by, for phrase-style proximity matching). `to_tsquery('english', 'fox & run')` builds that tree from the syntax you give it, and it stems the query's own words the same way `to_tsvector` stems documents. That is why searching for `'running'` can match a document containing only `'run'`: both sides are reduced to the same lexeme before comparison.

```sql
SELECT * FROM articles
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'fox & run');
```

`@@` is the match operator: it tests whether a `tsquery` is satisfied by a `tsvector` and returns a boolean. Writing `&`/`|`/`!` syntax by hand suits queries built in code, but it is the wrong tool for raw input from a search box, since `to_tsquery` expects that syntax and raises a syntax error on punctuation or spacing it doesn't recognize. `plainto_tsquery('english', 'running foxes')` is built for that input: it takes raw multi-word text, ignores punctuation, stems each word, and ANDs the results, with no risk of a syntax error. For search boxes that should also support quoted phrases or the word `or`, `websearch_to_tsquery` parses a small, forgiving query language that sits between the strict `tsquery` syntax and plain AND-only behavior.

sections.heading: Indexing: GIN on a Generated tsvector Column
sections.body:
Calling `to_tsvector('english', body)` inside the `WHERE` clause re-processes the whole body of every row on every search. It also means no index can help, because there is no stored value to index, only an expression computed on the fly. The standard fix is to store the computed `tsvector` once, as its own column, using a **generated column** (PostgreSQL 12+):

```sql
CREATE TABLE articles (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    body TEXT NOT NULL,
    search_vector TSVECTOR GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED
);

CREATE INDEX idx_articles_search ON articles USING GIN (search_vector);
```

The generated column is recomputed whenever `body` changes and stored like any other column, so it is computed once per write instead of once per read. A GIN index on it lets `@@` queries find matching rows through the index instead of re-stemming every body at query time:

```sql
SELECT * FROM articles WHERE search_vector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'fox & run');
```

An alternative that avoids the extra column is an **expression index** on the computed expression, `CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', body))`. The query must then use that same expression to match the index, and `to_tsvector` still runs on every write for index maintenance, though not on every read. The generated-column approach is generally preferred in modern PostgreSQL because it gives you a real column to query, instead of requiring every query to repeat the same expression.

sections.heading: Ranking Results with ts_rank
sections.body:
`@@` is boolean: a row matches or it doesn't, with no sense of *how well*, and rows come back in whatever order the planner produces, which is not 'best matches first.' For a search feature, relevance ordering matters as much as matching. `ts_rank(search_vector, query)` computes a relevance score from factors like how many of the query's terms appear and how often, and you sort by it explicitly:

```sql
SELECT id, title, ts_rank(search_vector, query) AS rank
FROM articles, to_tsquery('english', 'fox & run') AS query
WHERE search_vector @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

`ts_rank_cd` is a related function that also accounts for **cover density**, how close together the matching terms are, which can be a better signal for longer documents. A commonly missed refinement is **weighting** fields before combining them into one search vector: `setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B')` marks title matches with a higher weight category ('A') than body matches ('B'), and `ts_rank` takes those weights into account, so a term in an article's title outranks the same term appearing once deep in the body. A plain concatenation of title and body would lose that distinction.

Ranking is a separate cost from matching. The GIN index speeds up finding the *set* of matching rows through `@@`, but computing `ts_rank` for every row in that set and sorting by it is extra work done after the index has finished. A query with a huge number of matches still pays to rank and sort all of them, however fast the index made the initial match. To show users why a row matched, `ts_headline('english', body, query)` returns a text snippet with the matching terms wrapped in `<b>` tags. As with `ts_rank`, run it only on the rows you are about to display (after `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`), because it re-parses the original text and is slow if applied to every match.

examples.title: Why LIKE Over-Matches and Under-Matches at the Same Time
examples.code:
-- Over-matching: LIKE has no concept of word boundaries.
SELECT name FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%cat%';
-- matches 'Cat Tree', but ALSO 'Concatenated Cable Kit' and 'Category Sign'

-- Under-matching: LIKE has no stemming.
SELECT title FROM articles WHERE title ILIKE '%runs%';
-- misses an article titled 'Running in the Rain' entirely --
-- 'runs' is not a literal substring of 'Running'

-- Full-text search handles both correctly:
SELECT title FROM articles
WHERE to_tsvector('english', title) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'run');
-- matches 'Running in the Rain' (stemmed to the same lexeme, 'run'),
-- and does NOT match unrelated words that merely contain similar letters
examples.explanation: ILIKE '%cat%' has no notion of a whole word. It matches the substring 'cat' anywhere, including inside 'Concatenated' and 'Category', which a search feature shouldn't return. In the other direction, ILIKE '%runs%' needs that exact substring, so a title using 'Running' is missed even though the searcher means the same thing. Full-text search fixes both through one mechanism: to_tsvector breaks text into whole lexemes (so 'Concatenated' is one unrelated lexeme, not a partial match for 'cat'), and stemming normalizes 'Running' and 'runs' to the same root, 'run', so a tsquery for 'run' matches both without the over-matching or under-matching LIKE produces.

examples.title: Building and Querying a tsvector with plainto_tsquery
examples.explanation: plainto_tsquery takes the free-text phrase a user might type into a search box and does two things for you: it drops 'for' as a stop word (using the same stop-word list as to_tsvector), and it stems 'searching' and 'queries' to 'search' and 'queri', then combines them with AND. That is why a multi-word phrase typed by an end user can go into plainto_tsquery without any risk of a syntax error, unlike to_tsquery, which expects the caller to supply &/|/! operators between terms and can reject unexpected punctuation in raw input.

examples.title: Generated Column, GIN Index, and Ranked Results
examples.explanation: search_vector combines title and body into one searchable column, but setweight marks title-derived lexemes as category 'A' and body-derived lexemes as 'B' before they are combined with ||. An article with 'fox' in its title therefore ranks above one that mentions 'fox' once in a long body, because ts_rank takes the weight categories into account. Because search_vector is a GENERATED ... STORED column, it is recomputed whenever title or body changes and stored physically, so the GIN index on it accelerates the @@ match against already-processed data instead of recomputing to_tsvector on every query. Note that ORDER BY rank DESC LIMIT 5 still has to compute ts_rank and sort every row the @@ match returned before the top 5 can be picked. The index makes finding the matching set fast; ranking and sorting that set is separate work on top.

misconceptions.description: to_tsquery and plainto_tsquery are interchangeable ways of writing the same query -- just pick whichever one comes to mind.
misconceptions.clarification: to_tsquery expects structured syntax with &, |, or ! operators between terms, and raises a syntax error on arbitrary punctuation or spacing in raw input, so it is meant for queries built in code with a known structure. plainto_tsquery accepts raw free text (what a user types into a search box), ignores punctuation, stems each word, and ANDs the results with no risk of a syntax error, but it can't express OR or phrase matching from the input text. Passing unpredictable user input to to_tsquery risks runtime errors that plainto_tsquery (or websearch_to_tsquery, for input that should support quotes and OR) is designed to avoid.

misconceptions.description: A GIN index on a tsvector column means every full-text search query against that data is automatically fast, including the ranking and sorting step.
misconceptions.clarification: The GIN index accelerates the @@ match, finding which rows satisfy a tsquery by looking up lexemes instead of scanning every row. Ranking those matches with ts_rank (or ts_rank_cd) and sorting by the result is additional work done on the rows the index already found, and the index doesn't speed it up. A query that matches a very large number of rows still pays to compute and sort ranks for all of them, however quickly the index found the set. The index solves the matching problem, not the ranking problem.

exercises.prompt: Add full-text search to a `products(id, name, description)` table: create a generated tsvector column that weights `name` matches above `description` matches, index it for fast lookups, and write a ranked query for the search term 'wireless keyboard' typed by a user into a search box.
hints: setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') and setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B') combined with || give name matches a higher weight category than description matches.
Use a GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED column so search_vector is computed automatically and stored physically, then index that column with GIN.
Since the search term comes directly from a user-typed search box rather than structured &/| syntax, plainto_tsquery (or websearch_to_tsquery) is the safer choice over to_tsquery.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The generated search_vector column combines name and description into one searchable value, and setweight tags name-derived lexemes as 'A' and description-derived ones as 'B' before they are concatenated with ||, so ts_rank scores a product whose name contains 'keyboard' higher than one that only mentions it in a long description. The GIN index on search_vector lets the @@ match in the WHERE clause find candidate rows without scanning and re-stemming every row's text per query. plainto_tsquery is used because 'wireless keyboard' is raw search-box text with no &/| syntax: it stems and ANDs the two words safely, without the syntax-error risk to_tsquery has on unpredictable input.

exercises.prompt: A table has a GIN index built on a generated column `search_vector TSVECTOR GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED`, but this query still does a sequential scan instead of using the index. Explain why, and fix it.
hints: The index was built on the search_vector column, but this query computes to_tsvector(body) freshly inline instead of referencing search_vector at all -- are those guaranteed to be the same thing the index can use?

to_tsvector(body) with no config argument uses whatever the session's default text search configuration is, which may not be 'english'. The same mismatch risk applies to to_tsquery('running & foxes') with no config argument.
Rewrite the query to filter on the search_vector column directly, using the same 'english' configuration the generated column itself uses.
exercises.solutionCode:
SELECT * FROM articles
WHERE search_vector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'running & foxes');
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original query filters on the expression to_tsvector(body), computed inline, not on the search_vector column the GIN index was built on. Even though search_vector is defined as to_tsvector('english', body), the query never references it, so PostgreSQL can't use that index and computes to_tsvector(body) for every row in a sequential scan. There is a second latent problem to fix at the same time: leaving out the configuration argument (to_tsvector(body) and to_tsquery('running & foxes')) relies on the session's default text search configuration, which may differ from the 'english' configuration search_vector was built with. If the two sides disagree on stemming rules, legitimate matches can be missed even after the query references search_vector. Filtering on search_vector directly, with to_tsquery('english', ...) matching the generated column's own configuration, restores the index and removes the mismatch risk.

assessments.prompt: Why does a search for 'run' correctly match a document containing only the word 'running' under PostgreSQL full-text search, when `ILIKE '%run%'` would need the literal substring to be present?
options: Full-text search ignores the specific word entirely and matches based only on document length.

ILIKE '%run%' would actually match 'running' too, since 'run' is a literal substring of 'running'; the real difference only appears with word forms like 'runs' searched as '%runs%', and stemming plays no part.
PostgreSQL automatically converts every ILIKE query into a full-text search query behind the scenes.
to_tsvector and to_tsquery both apply the same stemming process to their input, reducing 'running' and 'run' to the identical normalized lexeme before any comparison happens.
assessments.explanation: to_tsvector stems document text and to_tsquery stems query text using the same configuration's stemming dictionary, so 'run' and 'running' reduce to one lexeme, and the @@ match compares those normalized forms instead of the literal words. The “PostgreSQL automatically converts every ILIKE query into…” option is false; ILIKE is never converted to full-text search, and they are separate mechanisms you choose between. The “Full-text search ignores the specific word entirely…” option is fabricated: ranking may consider term frequency, but matching is about specific lexemes, not document length. The “ILIKE '%run%' would actually match 'running' too…” option is a fair observation about this one example, since 'run' is a substring of 'running', but it doesn't explain the stemming mechanism and misses the case where it matters: searching '%runs%' against a document containing only 'running', where ILIKE fails and full-text search succeeds through stemming.

assessments.prompt: Explain how tsvector, tsquery, and the @@ operator work together to support full-text search, why a GIN index on a generated tsvector column matters for performance at scale, and why ranking with ts_rank is a distinct concern from matching.
assessments.modelAnswer: to_tsvector transforms a document's text into a tsvector: lowercasing, removing stop words that carry little search value, and stemming each remaining word to a shared root, while recording each lexeme's position for later proximity-aware features. to_tsquery (or the friendlier plainto_tsquery for raw user input) builds a tsquery from search terms using the same stemming, which is why a query for 'running' can match a document whose tsvector only contains the lexeme 'run': both sides are reduced to the same form before comparison, and a literal substring match like LIKE has nothing equivalent. The @@ operator then tests whether a tsquery's logical structure (its ANDed, ORed, or negated lexemes) is satisfied by a tsvector and returns a boolean. None of this solves the performance problem on a large table by itself: recomputing to_tsvector on raw text in a WHERE clause reprocesses every row's text on every search, with nothing to index. Storing the transformation once, as a generated column (GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector(...)) STORED) that is recomputed only when the source text changes, gives PostgreSQL a real column to build a GIN index on. GIN indexes the individual lexemes in each stored tsvector, so an @@ query against that column looks up matching rows instead of scanning and reprocessing every row. Ranking is a separate concern layered on top: @@ only answers yes or no per row, so without an explicit ordering, matched rows come back in whatever order the plan produces, which is not best-first. ts_rank computes a relevance score per matched row, optionally informed by field weighting through setweight so a title match can outrank the same term appearing once in a long body, and that score has to be computed and sorted across every row in the matched set. The GIN index makes finding the set fast but gives no shortcut for scoring and sorting it, so a query that matches a very large number of rows still pays a separate cost for ranking.

assessments.prompt: `to_tsvector('english', 'The quick foxes were running through the forest')` produces lexemes for 'forest', 'fox', 'quick', and 'run', but nothing at all for 'The', 'were', or 'through'. Why?
options: Those specific words failed to reduce to any valid stemmed root, so PostgreSQL silently treated the stemming step as an error and dropped them.
'The', 'were', and 'through' are common stop words carrying little search value.
to_tsvector has a maximum limit on the number of lexemes it stores per document, and those three words happened to be discarded to stay under that limit.
to_tsvector only processes the first and last words of each sentence, discarding whatever falls in between that isn't a noun.
assessments.explanation: This is the stop-word removal step: to_tsvector drops common words like 'the', 'were', and 'through' that occur so often they have no search value and would match nearly every document. The “to_tsvector has a maximum limit…” option invents a lexeme-count limit that isn't the mechanism here. The “Those specific words failed to reduce…” option fabricates a stemming failure; stemming doesn't fail and drop words, and stop-word removal and stemming are separate, deterministic steps. The “to_tsvector only processes the first and last…” option invents a position-based rule; to_tsvector processes every word and removes only those on the stop-word list.

assessments.prompt: A search feature passes raw, user-typed input like `running, foxes!!` directly into `to_tsquery('english', ...)` instead of `plainto_tsquery`. What's the likely problem?
options: to_tsquery expects already-structured syntax with explicit &, |, or ! operators between terms.
No problem -- to_tsquery and plainto_tsquery behave identically no matter what format the input text takes.
to_tsquery requires its input to already be a valid tsvector value, so passing any plain string at all always fails.
to_tsquery silently strips all punctuation and behaves exactly like plainto_tsquery in every situation, so there is no actual difference in outcome.
assessments.explanation: to_tsquery is built for structured query syntax and can reject raw punctuation it doesn't expect, while plainto_tsquery exists to accept free-text, user-typed input without that syntax-error risk. The “No problem -- to_tsquery and plainto_tsquery behave…” option contradicts the reason both functions exist with different intended inputs. The “to_tsquery silently strips all punctuation and behaves…” option overstates to_tsquery's tolerance; it does not behave like plainto_tsquery, and its handling of unexpected punctuation is the risk in question. The “to_tsquery requires its input to already…” option is false: to_tsquery accepts plain text in its expected syntax, not only pre-built tsvector values.

assessments.prompt: A `search_vector` column is built as `setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B')`. Two articles both contain the term 'python' exactly once -- one in its title, the other only in its body. Ranked by ts_rank, which one scores higher, and why?
options: Both articles are excluded from the ranked results entirely, because setweight requires the search term to appear in both title and body for a row to qualify at all.
The article with 'python' in its body scores higher, since category 'B' is processed before category 'A' in ts_rank's default evaluation order.

The article with 'python' in its title scores higher, because setweight tags title-derived lexemes with a higher weight category ('A') than body-derived lexemes ('B'), and ts_rank factors those weight categories into its computed relevance score.
Neither -- ts_rank ignores setweight entirely and scores purely on raw term frequency, so both articles receive an identical score.
assessments.explanation: setweight marks which part of a combined tsvector came from which source field using a weight category, and ts_rank uses those categories (weighting 'A' more heavily than 'B') when computing its score, so a title match outranks an equivalent body-only match. The “Neither -- ts_rank ignores setweight entirely…” option is false; using weight categories in the score is what setweight and ts_rank are designed to do together. The “The article with 'python' in its body…” option invents an evaluation-order rule with no basis in how ts_rank works. The “Both articles are excluded from the ranked…” option is fabricated: setweight has no requirement that the term appear in every field, and only affects scoring, not whether a row matches.

concepts.title: PostgreSQL Extensions: pg_trgm, uuid-ossp, and the Extension Model
concepts.description: PostgreSQL keeps its core small and ships specialized functionality, such as fuzzy string matching and UUID generation, as opt-in extensions enabled per database with CREATE EXTENSION. pg_trgm and uuid-ossp are two of the most commonly used, and each shows something different about what an extension changes and costs.
learningObjectives: Explain what a PostgreSQL extension is architecturally, and why CREATE EXTENSION is required rather than a feature simply being available by default.
Install and use pg_trgm for trigram-based fuzzy string similarity matching.
Use pg_trgm with a GIN index to accelerate leading-wildcard ILIKE queries and similarity searches that a plain B-tree index cannot support.
Explain what uuid-ossp (and the built-in gen_random_uuid) provide, and the concrete performance trade-off of random UUID primary keys versus sequential integers.
Explain the operational implications of relying on an extension: privilege requirements, per-database installation, and availability limits on managed PostgreSQL.

sections.heading: What an Extension Is
sections.body:
PostgreSQL's core is deliberately small, and a wide range of more specialized functionality (extra data types, functions, operators, and index operator classes) ships as **extensions**: self-contained bundles of SQL objects that can be installed, but must be enabled on a *specific database* with `CREATE EXTENSION extension_name;` before any of their objects can be used there. That is a design choice, not an oversight: a lean default installation means a database that never needs fuzzy matching or specialized UUID functions pays nothing for them, in installed objects, catalog entries, or surface area, while databases that need them opt in with one statement.

`\dx` in `psql` lists the extensions installed in the connected database, and the `pg_available_extensions` view lists every extension the server *could* install. Extensions have their own version numbers, separate from the server's, and are upgraded with `ALTER EXTENSION extension_name UPDATE;`, so a server upgrade and an extension upgrade are two operations, each possibly needed on its own schedule.

sections.heading: pg_trgm: Fuzzy Matching via Trigrams
sections.body:
`pg_trgm` (trigram matching) breaks a string into overlapping sequences of three consecutive characters ('cat' becomes `'  c'`, `' ca'`, `'cat'`, `'at '`, including boundary padding) and measures the similarity of two strings by how many trigrams they share. That gives you fuzzy matching: a string with a typo or minor variation still shares most of its trigrams with the correct spelling, so the score stays high where an exact or prefix match would fail.

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm;

SELECT similarity('postgres', 'postgre');   -- 0.7

SELECT name FROM products WHERE name % 'iphne';
-- the % operator: "is this similar enough to match", using the
-- pg_trgm.similarity_threshold setting (default 0.3) -- catches
-- rows like 'iPhone' that an exact match would miss
```

Beyond fuzzy matching, pg_trgm solves a problem from the indexing module: a leading-wildcard `ILIKE '%term%'` cannot use a standard B-tree index, because 'contains this substring anywhere' has no contiguous range in a B-tree's sorted order. pg_trgm provides a GIN (or GiST) **operator class** that indexes a column's trigrams, which *can* accelerate that pattern:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_products_name_trgm ON products USING GIN (name gin_trgm_ops);

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%phone%';
-- Bitmap Index Scan using idx_products_name_trgm
```

This is a different capability from a plain B-tree, not a faster version of the same thing: an extension adding a new *index operator class* that PostgreSQL's core indexing didn't offer before it was installed. One limit to know: a pattern shorter than three characters yields no trigrams to look up, so `ILIKE '%ab%'` still ends up scanning.

sections.heading: uuid-ossp and the UUID vs Sequential-Integer Trade-off
sections.body:
Historically, generating random UUIDs for primary keys required `CREATE EXTENSION "uuid-ossp";` for its `uuid_generate_v4()` function. PostgreSQL 13 and later ship `gen_random_uuid()` in core, so the extension is no longer needed for that purpose. `uuid-ossp` remains common in older codebases, so recognize it on sight instead of assuming it does something core can't.

The more consequential question has nothing to do with which function generates the value: UUIDs versus sequential integers (`BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`) as a primary key. UUIDs have real advantages. They are globally unique with no coordination, which matters when merging records generated independently across services, offline clients, or database shards, and they don't expose a guessable running count of rows the way an integer id in a URL does. Random UUIDs (the common v4 variant) have a measurable cost, though: each new value is random, so inserts land at scattered positions throughout the B-tree primary key index instead of appending at the end like a sequential bigint. That causes more index page splits, more bloat over time, and worse cache locality for recently inserted rows. **UUID v7**, a newer time-ordered variant, is a middle ground: it keeps UUID's coordination-free uniqueness but encodes a timestamp so successive values roughly increase, restoring much of the append-friendly locality that random v4 gives up. Check your PostgreSQL version for a built-in generator (recent releases add one); older versions need a library or the application to generate v7 values.

sections.heading: Operational Reality: Extensions Aren't Always Available
sections.body:
`CREATE EXTENSION` typically requires superuser privileges on a self-managed installation, or, for extensions marked *trusted* (since PostgreSQL 13, this includes pg_trgm), `CREATE` privilege on the database. An ordinary application role can't run it for most extensions, for good reason: some extensions can execute arbitrary code or reach the filesystem. Managed cloud PostgreSQL services are stricter still: providers typically allow only an approved list of extensions, and some are unavailable on certain tiers or plans whatever your privileges.

So 'which extension does this feature need' is as much an infrastructure and procurement question as a code decision. Verify an extension's availability on your hosting platform *before* designing a feature that depends on it. Remember that `CREATE EXTENSION` is scoped to one database, not the cluster: a multi-database cluster needs it enabled separately in each database that uses it. And `pg_dump` records which extensions a database relies on, so restoring that dump onto a fresh instance needs the same extensions to be installable there, which can surface an availability gap during a migration or disaster-recovery restore if nobody checked beforehand.

examples.title: pg_trgm Similarity and Fuzzy Matching
examples.explanation: similarity() returns a number reflecting how many trigrams two strings share. 'iphone' and 'iphne' share four of the nine distinct trigrams they have between them, a moderate score of about 0.44, while 'iphone' and 'android' share none, so the score is 0. The % operator turns this into a filter: it matches rows whose similarity to the search term exceeds a configurable threshold (pg_trgm.similarity_threshold, default 0.3). That is what lets a search box tolerate common typos and still surface the intended product, which neither an exact match nor a LIKE/ILIKE query can do. Note that a short word with a typo can fall under the default threshold: 'iphone' versus 'ihpone' scores only about 0.27, so you may need to lower the threshold for short strings (`SET pg_trgm.similarity_threshold = 0.2;` for the session). For ranked fuzzy lookups you can also sort by the distance operator, `ORDER BY name <-> 'iphne' LIMIT 5`, which a GiST trigram index can serve directly.

examples.title: GIN + pg_trgm Turns a Leading-Wildcard ILIKE Into an Index Scan
examples.explanation: A plain B-tree index on name can't help a leading-wildcard ILIKE pattern, since 'contains this substring anywhere' has no contiguous range in a B-tree's sorted order, so PostgreSQL falls back to a sequential scan. The gin_trgm_ops operator class, provided by the pg_trgm extension, indexes each row's trigrams, and a GIN index built with it can find candidate rows for a substring pattern without checking every row. That capability did not exist in PostgreSQL's indexing toolkit before the extension was installed; it is not a faster version of an existing one.

examples.title: uuid-ossp vs. Built-in gen_random_uuid, and the Insert-Locality Cost
examples.explanation: uuid_generate_v4() and gen_random_uuid() produce the same kind of value, a random UUID, so the choice between the uuid-ossp extension and the built-in function comes down to PostgreSQL version, not to any difference in the values. The insertion-pattern comment is the part to take away. A sequential bigint identity guarantees every new key is larger than every existing one, so inserts always extend the primary key's B-tree at one edge, close to the cheapest insertion pattern for a B-tree. A random UUID can sort anywhere relative to existing values, so inserts land scattered throughout the index, which is the mechanism behind the extra page splits and worse cache locality of random UUID primary keys at high insert volume.

misconceptions.description: Extensions are third-party add-ons, somehow less trustworthy or less 'real PostgreSQL' than built-in, core features.
misconceptions.clarification: Many of the extensions developers reach for most often (pg_trgm, uuid-ossp, pgcrypto, pg_stat_statements) are bundled with the standard PostgreSQL distribution in its contrib collection and maintained to the same standard as core. They are opt-in to keep the default installation small and to avoid imposing the cost of unused functionality (catalog entries, surface area, and in some cases security considerations for extensions that can touch the filesystem or run arbitrary code) on every database, not because they are less official or less carefully built than anything in core. `pg_stat_statements`, for example, is the usual first stop when you need to find which queries consume the most time in a running system.

misconceptions.description: Switching a primary key from a sequential bigint/identity column to a UUID is a purely cosmetic choice with no real performance implications, as long as both are technically unique.
misconceptions.clarification: A random (v4) UUID inserted as a primary key lands at a scattered position in the B-tree index on every insert, instead of appending at one edge like a sequential bigint identity. That causes measurably more index page splits, more bloat over time, and worse cache locality for recently inserted rows at high insert volume. It is an operational cost, not a stylistic preference, and one reason time-ordered alternatives like UUID v7 exist: they keep UUID's coordination-free global uniqueness while restoring an append-friendly insertion pattern.

exercises.prompt: Enable pg_trgm, create an index on `products.name` that would accelerate a leading-wildcard ILIKE search, and write a query that finds products similar to the misspelled search term 'wireles keybord' using the similarity operator.
exercises.code:
-- products: id BIGINT, name TEXT
-- Enable pg_trgm, add an appropriate index, and write the fuzzy-match query.
hints: CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm; makes both the similarity() function and the % operator available, and provides the gin_trgm_ops operator class for indexing.
CREATE INDEX ... USING GIN (name gin_trgm_ops) is what lets both leading-wildcard ILIKE and similarity queries use an index instead of a full scan.
The % operator filters by a similarity threshold directly -- it's the fuzzy-matching equivalent of an equality comparison.
exercises.solutionExplanation: CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm makes the trigram similarity() function, the % operator, and the gin_trgm_ops index operator class available in this database. The GIN index built with gin_trgm_ops indexes each row's trigrams, which accelerates both leading-wildcard ILIKE patterns and % similarity filtering, neither of which a plain B-tree index on name can support. The query uses % to keep rows similar enough to the misspelled term (above the default similarity threshold) and orders by the similarity() score, so the closest matches, likely a product named 'Wireless Keyboard', come first even though both words in the search term are misspelled.

exercises.prompt: A team migrates `orders.id` from `BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` to a randomly-generated UUID, expecting better scalability for a high-insert-volume table, but observes write throughput get noticeably worse afterward, along with growing index bloat. Explain why, and suggest two possible responses.
hints: Where in the primary key's B-tree index does each new value land under the old bigint identity scheme, versus under the new random UUID scheme?
A value that lands at a random, unpredictable position in an index (rather than always at one edge) tends to cause more index page splits as the tree rebalances -- how does that show up over time?

Consider whether the team actually needed UUID's specific properties (coordination-free global uniqueness, not leaking a row count) for this table, and whether a time-ordered UUID variant could give some of those benefits without the same insertion-locality cost.
exercises.solutionCode:
-- Response 1: if global, coordination-free uniqueness genuinely isn't
-- needed for this table, revert to a sequential identity column:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
);

-- Response 2: if UUID's properties ARE genuinely needed (e.g. ids
-- generated by multiple independent services without coordination),
-- use a time-ordered UUID variant (UUID v7) instead of a fully random
-- v4 UUID, which keeps successive values roughly increasing and
-- restores much of the sequential-key insertion locality.
exercises.solutionExplanation: A sequential bigint identity guarantees each new id is larger than every previous one, so every insert appends at one edge of the primary key's B-tree, close to the cheapest insertion pattern. A random (v4) UUID has no ordering: each new value lands at an unpredictable position throughout the index, which forces many more page splits as the tree makes room in the middle instead of at an edge. That explains both the drop in write throughput and the growing bloat after the migration. If the team switched for something UUIDs are good at (generating ids independently across services or offline clients without coordination, or avoiding a guessable sequential count in a public id), reverting would give that up unnecessarily, and a time-ordered scheme like UUID v7 is the more targeted fix: it keeps coordination-free global uniqueness while its timestamp component makes successive values trend upward, restoring much of the append-friendly pattern. If neither property was needed for this table, reverting to the sequential bigint identity is the simpler, correct response.

assessments.prompt: Why does installing the pg_trgm extension specifically matter for making `WHERE name ILIKE '%phone%'` fast, rather than this being something any sufficiently well-built B-tree index could eventually support?
options: ILIKE queries are always slow in PostgreSQL unless pg_trgm is installed, even with an exact prefix match and no wildcards at all.
pg_trgm makes PostgreSQL's existing B-tree index type faster at leading-wildcard searches through internal optimizations.

pg_trgm provides a genuinely different index operator class (gin_trgm_ops) that indexes a column's overlapping three-character sequences, which is a structurally different capability a B-tree's single sorted ordering cannot provide, regardless of how well-built it is.
pg_trgm works by automatically rewriting ILIKE queries into equivalent LIKE queries that a B-tree can handle.
assessments.explanation: A leading-wildcard pattern has no contiguous range in a B-tree's single sorted order, however the B-tree is built or tuned; that is a structural limit of the data structure, not a tuning gap. pg_trgm solves it by providing a different kind of index content (trigrams) through its own GIN/GiST operator class, a new capability and not a faster B-tree. The “pg_trgm makes PostgreSQL's existing B-tree index type…” option puts the mechanism in the B-tree instead of in a different index structure. The “ILIKE queries are always slow in PostgreSQL…” option overstates it: a pattern with no leading wildcard (LIKE 'phone%') can already use a standard B-tree index without any extension. The “pg_trgm works by automatically rewriting ILIKE queries…” option is fabricated; pg_trgm doesn't rewrite queries into a different operator.

assessments.prompt: Explain the PostgreSQL extension model in general terms, then use the UUID-versus-bigint primary key trade-off as a concrete case study of how an extension (or a feature it historically provided) can change what's possible, and at what cost.
assessments.modelAnswer: PostgreSQL keeps its core minimal and ships a lot of specialized functionality (additional data types, functions, operators, and index operator classes) as extensions: self-contained bundles of SQL objects that exist on the server but aren't active in a database until enabled there with CREATE EXTENSION. A database that doesn't need a piece of functionality pays nothing for it, and one that does opts in with a single statement. Many of the most used extensions, including pg_trgm and uuid-ossp, are bundled with PostgreSQL's own distribution and maintained to the same standard as core, so they are not third-party or lesser-trusted code. The UUID-versus-bigint case study shows two lessons. First, uuid-ossp historically provided uuid_generate_v4() as the standard way to generate random UUID keys, and that functionality has since been absorbed into core as the built-in gen_random_uuid() in version 13 and later, so what once required an extension no longer does, though the older function remains common in existing code. Second, and more consequential, the underlying design decision, UUID or sequential bigint as primary key, carries a structural performance trade-off whichever function generates the UUID. A sequential bigint identity guarantees each new value is larger than all previous ones, so inserts append at one edge of the primary key's B-tree, close to the cheapest insertion pattern. A random UUID has no ordering guarantee, so each new value lands at a scattered position in the index, causing more page splits, more bloat, and worse cache locality at meaningful insert volume. That cost is easy to overlook if UUID adoption is treated as 'just switching the id type' and not as an architectural trade-off: you gain coordination-free global uniqueness and non-guessable ids and pay with worse index insertion behavior, a trade-off that time-ordered schemes like UUID v7 soften by keeping global uniqueness while restoring much of the sequential key's append-friendly locality.

assessments.prompt: A PostgreSQL server hosts three separate databases: app_db, reporting_db, and test_db. `CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm;` is run while connected to app_db. What's true about reporting_db and test_db afterward?
options: pg_trgm is enabled only in app_db -- CREATE EXTENSION is scoped to the specific database it's run against.
pg_trgm is now automatically available in all three databases, since extensions are installed once at the entire server/cluster level.
Extensions can only ever be installed in a database literally named 'postgres', and every other database must access it remotely.
Running CREATE EXTENSION in app_db permanently prevents that same extension from ever being installed in any other database in the same cluster.
assessments.explanation: CREATE EXTENSION applies to one database, not the whole cluster, so a multi-database server needs the statement run in each database that wants to use the extension's objects. The “pg_trgm is now automatically available in all…” option gets the scope wrong: extensions are per database, not per cluster. The “Extensions can only ever be installed…” option invents a restriction; any database can have CREATE EXTENSION run against it, subject to privilege. The “Running CREATE EXTENSION in app_db permanently prevents…” option is fabricated; databases in a cluster don't exclude each other this way.

assessments.prompt: A developer using their application's regular database role tries to run `CREATE EXTENSION some_extension;` on a managed cloud PostgreSQL service, and it fails. What is the most likely explanation, per this concept?
options: The extension must first be purchased separately from the PostgreSQL Global Development Group before it can be enabled on any server.
Extensions can only be created by the original author of that specific extension, verified through a license key tied to their account.
CREATE EXTENSION is deprecated syntax in all modern PostgreSQL versions and has been entirely replaced by ALTER DATABASE.
CREATE EXTENSION typically requires superuser privilege or a specifically granted privilege.
assessments.explanation: An application role typically lacks the privilege CREATE EXTENSION requires by default, and managed cloud providers commonly restrict which extensions can be installed at all, through an approved list, whatever the privileges. The “CREATE EXTENSION is deprecated syntax in all…” option is false; CREATE EXTENSION is current, standard PostgreSQL syntax. The “Extensions can only be created…” option invents an author-verification requirement that doesn't exist. The “The extension must first be purchased separately…” option is fabricated; PostgreSQL's bundled and community extensions aren't sold or licensed per install.

assessments.prompt: A system merges records generated independently by many offline mobile clients that may not sync with a central server for weeks at a time. Why is a UUID primary key a better fit for these records than a sequential BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY column?
options: UUIDs are mandated by the SQL standard for any table that might eventually be written to by more than one client.

A sequential IDENTITY column's values are only guaranteed unique within its own database's sequence -- two offline clients generating ids independently, with no coordination or connectivity between them, could easily produce colliding values; a UUID's effectively unique value space makes independent generation safe without requiring any coordination at all.
Sequential IDENTITY columns cannot be used in any table that will later be queried by more than one application.
UUIDs are always faster to index than sequential integers, regardless of insertion pattern or table size.
assessments.explanation: A sequential identity column's uniqueness depends on one shared sequence, which offline, unsynced clients can't coordinate against, so their independently assigned ids are likely to collide when merged. A UUID's effectively unique value space makes independent generation across many clients safe by construction. The “UUIDs are always faster to index…” option is false in general: this concept describes UUIDs' insertion-locality cost compared with sequential integers. The “UUIDs are mandated by the SQL standard…” option invents a mandate that doesn't exist. The “Sequential IDENTITY columns cannot be used…” option is fabricated: identity columns are used constantly in systems with many clients and applications, and the issue here is independent, uncoordinated generation, not multi-client access in general.
